title: The Agent Spectrum: ReAct to Autonomous Loops
summary: Trace what each step up the agent spectrum adds and what it costs -- interleaved reasoning and acting, plan-then-execute, reflection across attempts, and loops that must persist across context windows -- using the research and runtime behavior that define each one.
objectives: Explain what ReAct changes about an agent's action space and name the failure modes the ReAct paper reports for interleaved reasoning and acting.
Contrast an observation-dependent loop with a plan-then-execute (ReWOO) design on token growth, behavior under tool failure, and the environments where upfront planning breaks down.
Describe how Reflexion turns a pass/fail signal into bounded episodic memory, and identify the trigger and trial limits that keep it from retrying without end.
Specify the termination rule, persistence artifacts, and start-of-session check a loop needs once it must survive a turn limit or a fresh context window.

sections.title: ReAct: a thought is an action that touches nothing
paragraphs: ReAct (Yao et al.) is the first rung above a single model call, and its central move is small: it adds language itself to the agent's action space. A thought is an action that does not affect the external environment and returns no observation; it only updates the context the next step conditions on. Interleaving thoughts with real actions -- search, lookup, and finish in the paper's simple Wikipedia API -- lets the model reason about what to retrieve next and use what it retrieves to revise its reasoning.

The paper uses thoughts at two densities. On knowledge tasks (HotpotQA question answering and FEVER fact verification) the trajectory alternates thought, action, and observation at every step. On long-horizon decision tasks (the ALFWorld text game and the WebShop shopping environment) the model decides for itself where sparse thoughts appear -- to decompose the goal, track which subgoals are done, and choose the next one. On those two decision benchmarks, one- or two-shot ReAct prompting outperformed imitation and reinforcement learning baselines by an absolute 34 and 10 points of success rate.

Grounding is not free, and the paper says so. In its human-labelled sample of HotpotQA trajectories, hallucination accounted for 56% of chain-of-thought failures and none of ReAct's, but reasoning errors made up 47% of ReAct's failures -- including a recurring pattern where the model repeats its previous thoughts and actions and cannot break out of the loop -- and non-informative search results caused 23% of its errors. ReAct scored slightly below chain-of-thought on HotpotQA (27.4 versus 29.4 exact match) while beating it on FEVER. The best prompting results combined the two: fall back from ReAct to self-consistent chain-of-thought when ReAct fails to answer within a fixed number of steps (7 for HotpotQA, 5 for FEVER).

ReAct, by Yao et al., adds language itself to the agent's action space. A thought is an action that does not affect the external environment and returns no observation. It only updates the context that the next step conditions on. Interleaving thoughts with real actions, such as search, lookup, and finish in the paper's Wikipedia interface, lets the model decide what to retrieve next and revise its response after seeing evidence.

The paper uses thoughts at two densities. On HotpotQA question answering and FEVER fact verification, trajectories alternate thought, action, and observation at every step. On the longer-horizon ALFWorld and WebShop decision tasks, thoughts appear more sparsely to decompose goals and track subgoals. The paper reports that one-shot or two-shot ReAct prompting improved success over imitation or reinforcement-learning baselines by 34 points on ALFWorld and 10 points on WebShop.

Grounding is not free. In the paper's human-labelled sample of HotpotQA failures, reasoning errors made up 47% of ReAct failures, including repeated thought-action loops, and non-informative search made up 23%. Hallucination accounted for 0% of ReAct failures in that sample, compared with 56% of chain-of-thought failures. ReAct scored 27.4 exact match on HotpotQA compared with 29.4 for chain-of-thought, while beating it on FEVER. The combined prompting method switched from ReAct to self-consistent chain-of-thought if ReAct did not answer within 7 steps on HotpotQA or 5 steps on FEVER.

In this module, a thought is represented only by a public decision summary. A summary states the observable decision and the evidence supporting it, such as, "The customer is confirmed OPEN, so inspect the incident next." It does not request or expose private chain-of-thought.
sections.callout: In ReAct's evaluation, a step limit was not only a stop condition. It could trigger a switch to a different strategy.

sections.title: ReWOO: plan first, observe later
paragraphs: An interleaved loop pays for its flexibility on every step. ReWOO's authors point out that a stateless model API has to be sent the whole history -- context prompt, exemplars, and every prior thought, action, and observation -- each time the loop resumes after a tool call, so input tokens grow roughly quadratically with the number of reasoning steps. ReWOO splits the loop into three modules: a Planner that writes a full blueprint of interdependent steps before any tool runs, Workers that execute the tool calls and fill in evidence placeholders, and a Solver that combines the plans and the evidence into an answer.

The paper reports 5x token efficiency and a 4-point accuracy gain on HotpotQA, and it is specific about why the observation-dependent baseline lost. In 100 sampled HotpotQA failures, a bad tool response often pushed ReAct into repetition -- tool A fails, it tries tool B, B fails, it returns to A -- until the token limit ended the run. When every tool was forced to return 'No evidence found', ReWOO degraded less than ReAct did.

The limit is just as concrete. When the environment reveals little before it is observed -- the paper's example is an ALFWorld room with dozens of drawers, shelves, and cabinets and a vase somewhere among them -- a planner that cannot look first must enumerate every possibility, and its plan becomes as long as the worst case of the observation-dependent loop it replaced. Plans can also be reasonable and still wrong: the authors show a plan that assumes a search result will contain a person's age when it does not.

An interleaved loop pays for its flexibility on every model step. ReWOO's authors explain that a stateless model API must receive the full history again whenever the loop resumes after a tool call. That history includes the context prompt, exemplars, and prior thoughts, actions, and observations. Summed across a growing trajectory, this produces roughly quadratic input-token growth.

ReWOO separates three roles. A Planner writes a blueprint with evidence placeholders such as #E1 through #Ek before tools run. Workers execute the declared calls and fill those placeholders. A Solver combines the plan and collected evidence to produce the answer. The paper reports 5x token efficiency and a 4-point HotpotQA accuracy improvement over its interleaved baseline.

The paper also describes retry oscillation in the interleaved baseline: one bad tool response leads to another tool, that tool fails, and the loop returns to the first tool until the token limit. When tools were forced to return no evidence, ReWOO degraded less than ReAct.

Plan-first execution has a concrete limit. In the paper's ALFWorld example, a vase may be hidden among many drawers, shelves, and cabinets. A planner that cannot observe first must enumerate the possibilities, making its plan approach a worst-case observation-dependent search. A reasonable plan can also assume evidence that a tool does not actually provide.
The simulation in this module is a deterministic teaching model. It is not a reproduction or validation of the paper's empirical results.

code.label: Control-flow and input-growth comparison
code.code:
Interleaved, ReAct-style
  call model with current history
  select one tool from current observations
  run tool and append observation
  stop on success or a hard inner-step limit

Plan-then-execute, ReWOO-style
  planner declares evidence slots before observations
  workers fill those slots without replanning
  solver evaluates all evidence
  stop on success or the worker limit

Typical trade-off
  interleaving adapts after each observation but resends growing history
  plan-first execution avoids observation-driven replanning but can commit to a bad plan

sections.title: Reflexion: learning across attempts without new weights
paragraphs: Reflexion (Shinn et al.) moves up a rung by wrapping a second loop around the first. An Actor -- the paper uses ReAct or chain-of-thought -- produces a trajectory. An Evaluator scores it, using exact-match grading, a hand-written heuristic, self-generated unit tests, or another model as judge. A Self-Reflection model turns that sparse score into a short verbal lesson, which is stored in episodic memory and given to the Actor on the next trial. Nothing is fine-tuned; the policy is the model plus its memory.

The bounds are part of the design, not an afterthought. Memory is capped at a small number of stored reflections (usually one to three) to stay inside the context window, and trials run up to a maximum count. In ALFWorld the paper triggers reflection with a plain heuristic: the same action producing the same observation for more than three cycles, or more than 30 actions in one environment. With that heuristic, ReAct plus Reflexion completed 130 of 134 ALFWorld tasks, while ReAct alone stopped improving between trials 6 and 7.

Reflexion is only as good as its evaluator and its search space. The authors note that it depends on the model's self-evaluation or on heuristics and carries no formal guarantee of success, and on WebShop they stopped after four trials because the agent's reflections were not producing improvement. Tasks that need diverse, creative exploration expose the local-minimum problem shared by any loop that optimizes a policy from its own experience.

Reflexion, by Shinn et al., wraps an outer loop around an Actor. The Actor can use ReAct or chain-of-thought. An Evaluator scores the trajectory using exact match, a heuristic, generated tests, or another model as judge. A Self-Reflection component turns the score into a short verbal lesson stored in episodic memory and supplied to the next trial.

The bounds are part of the architecture. The paper usually caps memory at one to three reflections and limits the number of trials. In ALFWorld, reflection was triggered when the same action produced the same observation for more than three cycles or when a trajectory exceeded 30 actions. ReAct with Reflexion solved 130 of 134 ALFWorld tasks, while ReAct alone plateaued between trials 6 and 7.

Reflexion depends on its evaluator and has no convergence guarantee. The paper reports stopping WebShop after four trials because performance did not improve. A misleading evaluator can reinforce the wrong lesson, and repeated self-reflection can remain trapped in a narrow search region.

Episodic memory is runtime data, not a model-weight update. A later attempt receives a stored lesson as input. Changing model weights would require a separate training procedure, which neither this exercise nor the Reflexion control loop claims to perform.
sections.callout: Bound the inner steps, number of trials, and memory length separately. A bound on only one of these does not bound the entire system.

sections.title: Autonomous loops: termination and persistence become the design
paragraphs: At the far end of the spectrum the loop runs long enough that its runtime rules matter more than its prompt. The OpenAI Agents SDK documents its loop plainly: call the current agent's model; if the output is final -- text of the desired type with no tool calls -- return it; on a handoff, switch agents and continue; on tool calls, execute them, append the results, and call the model again; and throw MaxTurnsExceededError when the turn limit is reached, unless the limit has been explicitly disabled. Every autonomous loop needs the same three answers: what counts as done, what counts as too long, and what happens in each case.

Anthropic's write-up on harnesses for long-running agents describes what breaks when work spans many context windows, even with context compaction: the agent tries to finish everything at once and runs out of context mid-feature; a later session sees partial progress and declares the job done; features get marked complete without end-to-end testing. The fix was environmental rather than a cleverer prompt. A first session writes an init script, a progress log, an initial git commit, and a JSON feature list with every feature marked failing. Every later session reads the log and the git history, runs a basic end-to-end check before starting, works on one feature at a time, and leaves a commit and a progress note behind. Coding sessions may change only a feature's pass status, and the authors chose JSON because the model was less likely to overwrite it inappropriately than a Markdown file.

The general lesson is that persistence belongs in artifacts the next session can verify, not in whatever survived summarization. A feature list whose only mutable field is pass or fail, a progress file, and version-control history give a fresh context window a ground truth to check itself against -- the same role the environment's observations play for a single ReAct step.

At the far end of the spectrum, runtime rules matter as much as prompts. The OpenAI Agents SDK documentation describes a loop in which final output with no tool calls terminates successfully, a handoff changes the active agent, and tool calls append observations before the model runs again. A configured turn limit raises MaxTurnsExceededError when exceeded unless that limit is disabled. Provider-neutral loop design asks the same questions: what counts as done, what counts as too long, and what happens at the limit?

Anthropic's long-running-agent harness write-up describes failures across context windows even when compaction is available. An agent may run out of context during a feature, a later session may mistake partial progress for completion, or a feature may be marked complete without an end-to-end test. The proposed harness writes initialization artifacts, a progress log, git history, and a JSON feature list initially marked failing. Later sessions inspect those artifacts and run checks before new work.

Persistence belongs in artifacts that a fresh session can verify. A summary is not enough. A restart check should load durable state, verify its identity and schema, inspect pending or unknown effects, and block blind repetition when an external effect may already have occurred.

The fictional lookup task in this module is read-only. Its tools do not create an external write, so there is no side effect to roll back. The persistence exercise also creates a separate blocked example with pending and unknown effect markers. That example demonstrates that a restart guard must stop before resumed work. It does not claim that deleting or editing a local JSON file reverses an external effect.
sections.callout: A restart check must distinguish confirmed, pending, and unknown effects before it resumes work.

sections.title: Pick the lowest rung whose failure the task can afford
paragraphs: Each rung buys something specific and charges for it. Interleaving buys grounding and traces a person can inspect, but it resends context on every step and can loop on bad observations. Plan-then-execute buys token efficiency and resilience to failing tools, but it needs an environment the planner can reason about before looking. Reflection buys improvement across attempts, but it needs an evaluator you trust and a task that can be reset and retried. Long-running persistence buys continuity across context windows, but it needs durable artifacts and a verification step that every session honors.

So the design question is not how autonomous the agent should be but which failure the task can afford. A task with a cheap, reliable checker and safe retries suits a reflection loop. A task whose steps are foreseeable and whose tools are unreliable suits a planner-worker-solver split. A task in an unfamiliar environment needs an observation at every step and a hard limit on how many steps it may take.

Each rung buys something specific and charges for it. Interleaving buys observation-dependent adaptation and an inspectable trace, but it resends context and can loop on bad observations. Plan-then-execute reduces repeated model context and can isolate tool work, but it requires a useful plan before evidence arrives. Reflection can improve later attempts, but it requires a trustworthy evaluator, safe resets, and explicit bounds. Long-running persistence provides continuity, but it requires durable artifacts and a restart check.

The design question is not how autonomous the agent can be. It is which failure the task can afford. A task with a cheap reliable checker and safe retries may suit reflection. A foreseeable task with unreliable tools may suit a planner-worker-solver split. An unfamiliar environment whose useful actions depend on each new observation may require interleaving.

The transfer principle is provider-neutral. The same control-flow choices apply to any runtime that can select a tool, receive an observation, evaluate a result, enforce bounds, and persist verifiable state. The exercise does not depend on a feature unique to any particular model vendor or cloud platform.
sections.callout: Choose architecture from the task's uncertainty, evaluator quality, retry safety, and failure cost, not from a product label.

sections.title: Worked case: confirm two OPEN records
paragraphs: The self-contained fictional task uses two read-only tools. customer_lookup(customer_id) returns a customer record or an empty list. incident_lookup(incident_id) returns an incident record, an error object, or an empty list. Success requires a customer record whose customer_id exactly matches the requested customer, an incident record whose incident_id exactly matches the requested incident, and status OPEN on both records.

The baseline input is customer_id C-17 and incident_id I-42. Both matching records are OPEN. The all-empty fault uses the same requested identifiers but makes both tools return an empty list. An empty list is a valid response from that call, not proof that the record is absent everywhere.

All three simulations use the same tools and success predicate. An inner step is one tool action followed by its observation. Planning, evaluation, reflection, memory updates, trial boundaries, solver calls, and termination events do not count as tool steps. Interleaved execution allows at most 5 steps. Planner-worker-solver execution allows at most 5 workers. Bounded reflection allows at most 2 trials with 5 inner steps per trial and at most 2 memory lessons.
Every architecture stops immediately when the exact success predicate passes. A wrong record identifier never satisfies the predicate merely because its status is OPEN.
sections.callout: Success is exact identity plus OPEN status for both requested records. Empty lists, errors, malformed values, wrong identifiers, and partial evidence all fail.

sections.title: Offline fixture file
paragraphs: Save this complete fixture as fixture.json. It contains the baseline, all-empty fault, independent changed input, wrong-identifier negative case, and malformed-value negative case.

The changed input is C-18 and I-43. Its customer is OPEN. Its incident tool returns a temporary error on the first call and an empty list on later calls. This is genuinely different from the all-empty task and must not be answered by copying the empty trace.

sections.title: Standard-library deterministic simulation
paragraphs: Save this complete program as simulation.py. It uses only the Python standard library. The architecture labels are analogies for teaching control flow, not claims that the program performs model reasoning or reproduces the source papers.

The tools are actually called by every architecture. Event traces, stop reasons, counters, evaluations, and reflection memory are built from runtime results. The checks cover exact identifiers, malformed types, empty observations, partial failure, input immutability, early success, inner limits, trial limits, growth arithmetic, and persistence restart guards.

sections.title: Interpret the successful, changed, and growth results
paragraphs: Baseline answer key: all three architectures call customer_lookup(C-17) at Step 1 and receive the matching OPEN customer. At Step 2 they call incident_lookup(I-42) and receive the matching OPEN incident. The evaluator passes and each architecture stops immediately. There is no Step 3 and no second reflection trial. Each result therefore has 2 tool steps, 2 observations, and reason success.

Independent changed-input task, attempt before reading the key: use C-18 and I-43. The customer is OPEN, but the incident first returns an error and later returns an empty list. Decide whether a retry is safe, identify the missing evidence, and apply each architecture's declared limit.

Changed-input key for interleaving: Step 1 customer_lookup(C-18) returns the matching OPEN customer. Steps 2 through 5 call incident_lookup(I-43). Step 2 returns the temporary error and Steps 3 through 5 return empty lists because the sequence is exhausted. The incident is never confirmed OPEN, so evaluation fails and termination is step_limit.

Changed-input key for planner-worker-solver: the fixed slots are customer, incident, customer, incident, customer. Step 1 confirms the customer. Step 2 receives the incident error. Step 3 repeats the customer slot. Step 4 receives the incident empty list. Step 5 repeats the customer slot. The Solver lacks a matching OPEN incident, so it fails with worker_limit.

Changed-input key for bounded reflection: Trial 1 confirms the customer, then receives one incident error followed by three empty incident observations. Evaluation fails and stores one lesson. Trial 2 starts with incident_lookup because memory changes the initial order. Its fresh runtime returns the incident error, then customer_lookup confirms the customer, and the remaining incident calls return empty lists. Trial 2 fails and termination is trial_limit. There is no third trial. The retry is safe only because these fictional tools are read-only.

The input-growth comparison uses declared synthetic character-units, not measured tokens, live prices, or benchmark costs. Fixed prompt plus question is 20 units. Each public decision summary is 8, action is 4, and observation is 12. Interleaved step i resends 20 + i times 24 units. The five inputs are 44, 68, 92, 116, and 140, totaling 460. Plan-first execution uses planner input 20, worker payloads 5 times 4 equals 20, and solver input 20 plus 5 times 12 equals 80. Its total is 120. The ratio is 460 divided by 120, which reduces to 23 divided by 6, approximately 3.8333. This arithmetic illustrates the declared model only.

Counterexample to planning first: if the task merely says that a vase is somewhere in an unfamiliar room, a planner cannot know before the first observation whether to inspect a drawer, shelf, or cabinet. A fixed plan must enumerate branches. An observation-dependent agent can use the first observation to narrow the next action.
sections.callout: The simulation validates its own deterministic control flow. It does not validate the ReAct, ReWOO, or Reflexion paper results.

sections.title: Negative cases, durable state, and feedback
paragraphs: The program's 46 assertions are reached only by calling the architecture functions, tool runtime, success predicate, arithmetic function, and persistence guards. The check count is derived from the number of completed checks. It is not printed without tests.

Wrong identifiers are meaningful negative cases. A record with status OPEN but customer_id C-999 cannot satisfy a request for C-17. Error objects and empty lists cannot satisfy the record-shape predicate. CLOSED status fails. A malformed scalar observation raises TypeError instead of reaching .get or being silently accepted.

Input immutability is tested by deep-copying the entire fixture before all architecture runs and asserting equality afterward. Tool observations are also deep-copied. Early success is tested by requiring all three baseline runs to stop at exactly 2 steps and requiring bounded reflection to use only one trial.

Persistence is exercised with actual JSON save and load operations in the folder selected by --data-dir. The read-only task has an empty effects list and may resume after identity and shape checks. The separate WRITE-DEMO state contains one pending and one unknown effect. Reloading it produces resume=False, so the program performs no resumed work for that task. A mismatched task identifier raises ValueError.

Graduated hints: first, write the exact success predicate before choosing a loop. Second, count only action-observation pairs as tool steps. Third, treat an empty observation as local evidence from one call, not global proof. Fourth, distinguish retry safety from evidence sufficiency. A read-only retry can be safe while still failing to establish success.

Specific feedback for interleaving: a sixth tool step violates the limit, and success on empty or wrong-identifier evidence violates the predicate. Specific feedback for planner-worker-solver: changing the declared slots after an observation creates a different, replanning architecture. Specific feedback for reflection: a third trial violates the trial bound, more than two lessons violates the exercise cap, and a reflection without an evaluation has no stated basis. Specific feedback for persistence: trusting a summary without loading state, checking task identity, and inspecting effects does not establish a safe restart.

Additional manual negative experiments are useful after the unchanged program passes. Change the malformed customer response to a nonempty list and confirm TypeError. Change a baseline identifier while leaving status OPEN and confirm success becomes false. Add a third reflection trial in the implementation and confirm the trial assertion must be updated or fails. Change an effect status to mystery and confirm load_state rejects it. Change readonly_state.json after writing but before loading so task_id differs and confirm the restart check blocks it.
This module supplies written teaching and facilitation material. It does not claim that a video or audio recording exists.
sections.callout: Do not simulate rollback by editing local state. Pending or unknown external effects require reconciliation with the real external system before retry.

activity.reflectionPrompt: Which rung did your task actually need, and which failure reported in the source papers would have appeared first if you had chosen the rung above it?

questions.prompt: In ReAct, what distinguishes a thought from an action such as search[entity]?
choices: A thought is executed by a separate, smaller model
A thought does not affect the environment and returns no observation; it only updates the context for later steps
A thought must always be followed by a finish action
A thought is removed from the trajectory before the next step
questions.explanation: ReAct augments the action space with language. A thought composes information over the current context and produces no observation feedback, while actions such as search and lookup interact with the environment.

questions.prompt: In the ReAct paper's human-labelled HotpotQA sample, which failure pattern did the authors identify as specific to ReAct?
choices: Hallucinated facts as the dominant failure mode
Refusing to answer when search results were empty
Repeating its previous thoughts and actions and failing to break out of the loop
Exceeding the context window on every question
questions.explanation: The paper reports a frequent ReAct-specific error in which the model repetitively generates previous thoughts and actions. Hallucination was the dominant chain-of-thought failure, at 56%, and accounted for none of ReAct's failures in that sample.

questions.prompt: Why do ReWOO's authors argue that interleaved reasoning-and-observation loops become expensive as tasks lengthen?
choices: A stateless API must be resent the full history each time the loop resumes, so total input tokens grow roughly quadratically with the number of steps
Tool providers charge more for each successive call
Thoughts are always longer than actions
Interleaved loops require fine-tuning before they can run
questions.explanation: Each resumed call carries the context prompt, exemplars, and prior thoughts, actions, and observations. ReWOO separates planning from worker execution so observations do not repeatedly enter the Planner's history.

questions.prompt: When does a plan-then-execute design like ReWOO lose its advantage over an observation-dependent loop?
choices: Whenever any tool returns an error
When the task has a single fixed answer
When the Solver receives evidence from more than one Worker
When the environment reveals little before it is observed, so the plan must enumerate every possibility
questions.explanation: The paper's ALFWorld example shows that a planner with little knowledge of the environment must plan for a worst case that can match the complexity of the observation-dependent loop.

questions.prompt: What keeps a Reflexion agent from growing its memory or retrying without end?
choices: It fine-tunes the model after each failed trial
Memory is capped, trials have a maximum count, and reflection is triggered by explicit conditions
The Evaluator must pass every trajectory after three trials
It discards all prior trajectories and reflections at each reset
questions.explanation: The paper usually bounds memory to one to three reflections, runs only up to a maximum trial count, and uses explicit triggers such as repeated action-observation cycles. Episodic memory is not fine-tuning.

questions.prompt: A long-running coding agent keeps declaring the project finished after partial progress. Which change from Anthropic's long-running harness write-up targets that failure?
choices: Raise the turn limit so the agent has more time
Rely on compaction summaries to carry project status
Run every session in parallel
Initialize a JSON feature list as failing and change pass status only after end-to-end testing
questions.explanation: The write-up pairs a JSON feature list, initially all failing, with progress artifacts and checks. Compaction alone was not sufficient.

sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations for Efficient Augmented Language Models
Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

cues.text: Begin with the distinction that defines ReAct. A language thought updates context but does not touch the environment and does not receive an observation. A tool action does touch an environment and returns evidence. This distinction matters because it lets us count and bound observable work without asking for private chain-of-thought. In class, use public decision summaries instead. A summary can say that the customer is confirmed and the incident should be checked next. It should not attempt to reveal hidden internal deliberation. Point out that ReAct used dense thought-action-observation alternation on HotpotQA and FEVER, but sparse thoughts on ALFWorld and WebShop. Then emphasize the reported failure modes. Grounding reduced hallucination in the paper's labelled sample, but it did not eliminate failure. ReAct still produced reasoning errors, repeated loops, and uninformative searches. A hard step limit therefore changes the architecture from an open-ended conversation into a bounded procedure.
Show a static three-column comparison of language update, tool action, and observation. Mark only tool action plus observation pairs as numbered inner steps.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A text table defines a language update as context-only, a tool action as an external call, and an observation as returned evidence. Numbered labels identify only action-observation pairs.

cues.text: Move to ReWOO by asking what the interleaved loop repeatedly pays for. In a stateless interface, each resumed model call includes the prior history again. If the history grows by a fixed amount per step, summing all those prefixes produces roughly quadratic total input growth. ReWOO changes control flow rather than merely shortening a prompt. The Planner declares evidence slots before tools run, Workers fill the slots, and the Solver combines plan and evidence. This can avoid feeding every observation back into the planning process. Keep the empirical result and the exercise separate. The paper reports its own token-efficiency and HotpotQA findings. Our Python program does not reproduce those findings. It only makes the structural difference inspectable. Also teach the counterexample: when useful actions depend on an observation that has not happened yet, a plan must enumerate branches or be revised. A fixed plan is not universally superior.

Ask learners to name a tool in their own environment that sometimes fails. Have them distinguish a declared retry slot from an observation-driven retry, then ask which one their task actually requires.

Introduce Reflexion as an outer loop. The Actor produces a bounded attempt. The Evaluator supplies a score or decision. Reflection converts that evaluation into a compact lesson, and episodic memory supplies the lesson to a later trial. Stress the word episodic. The memory is runtime input, not a change to the model's weights. A separate training procedure would be needed to update weights. Next separate three bounds that learners often collapse into one: inner tool steps per trial, total number of trials, and memory capacity. If only tool steps are bounded, repeated trials can still run without end. If trials are bounded but memory grows without limit, later contexts can still become unwieldy. Finally, discuss evaluator dependence. A reflection is not automatically correct merely because it sounds plausible. An unreliable evaluator can reward the wrong behavior, and the paper offers no convergence guarantee.
Allow two minutes for learners to write the evaluator they would trust for one task, one way that evaluator could be wrong, and the maximum trials they would permit.

Now extend the time horizon. Once work can survive a context window, a fresh session needs evidence that exists outside the prior conversation. Explain the three runtime decisions: what counts as success, what limit ends the run, and what state is durable enough to support restart. The OpenAI Agents SDK is one concrete documented loop, but the lesson transfers beyond that SDK. Final output, tool continuation, handoff, and turn exhaustion are control-flow events that every runtime must define in some form. Then connect this to the long-running harness account. Compaction did not make partial work trustworthy. Durable feature status, progress records, source history, and end-to-end checks gave later sessions something verifiable. For side effects, teach a stricter rule. Pending or unknown status must block blind repetition. A local file cannot undo an external write, so restart requires reconciliation or an idempotency check against the actual system.
Ask one learner to state a success rule, a limit, an at-limit result, a durable artifact, and a restart check as five separate design choices.

Synthesize the spectrum by matching each architecture to uncertainty. Interleaving is useful when the next action genuinely depends on the latest observation. Plan-first execution is useful when work is foreseeable and observations need not alter the declared plan. Reflection is useful when attempts are safely repeatable and evaluation is reliable enough to guide another trial. Persistence is required when a later session must distinguish completed, pending, and unknown work. More autonomy is not automatically better. Every additional loop adds another way to continue incorrectly. The practical rule is to select the lowest rung that handles the task's uncertainty and failure cost. This is provider-neutral. Any runtime with tools, observations, evaluation, limits, and files can implement the exercise's control flow.

Present the fictional task before showing code. Success requires two exact record identities and two OPEN statuses. This prevents a common evaluator bug in which any OPEN object is accepted. Explain that an empty list is a legitimate local response, not global proof that no record exists. Count only a tool call and its returned observation as one inner step. Planning, evaluation, termination, reflection, and memory updates remain visible but do not consume the tool-step allowance. Walk through the baseline prediction. Customer first, incident second, then immediate success. Ask learners to say why a third step would be fictitious. Next preview the empty fault. Every design sees the same inputs and tools, but its control structure determines which calls it makes, where evaluation occurs, and which limit supplies the stop reason.

Inspect the fixture as data rather than instructions. Baseline contains two matching OPEN records. Empty contains two empty responses. Changed contains a successful customer and a stateful incident sequence: first an error, then empty responses. Wrong_ids contains convincing-looking OPEN records with identities that do not match the request. Malformed contains a scalar where the tool contract permits only an object or empty list. Ask learners which cases fail because evidence is missing, which fail because identity is wrong, and which should raise before evaluation. This separation matters in production systems because a tool-contract violation should not be quietly converted into a normal negative answer.

Guide learners through the program from the predicate outward. is_record checks type, required fields, field types, and exact identity. is_open adds status. success requires both sides. ToolRuntime deep-copies responses and rejects malformed observations. The interleaved selector uses current evidence and call counts, so it actually makes observation-dependent decisions. The plan runner declares its complete slot order before any lookup and never changes that order. The reflection runner creates a fresh bounded trial, evaluates it, stores at most the allowed lessons, and changes only the initial read order on the second trial. None of these functions contains a language model, and their public decisions are deterministic labels. Finally, examine run_checks. It calls all three architectures on baseline, empty, and changed cases. It verifies early success, limits, errors, wrong identities, malformed types, immutability, arithmetic, and restart behavior before the success count is printed.

Give learners several minutes to create a local folder, paste both complete files, and run the program. Remind them that the data directory is their choice and that no network access or secret is needed. If their output differs, have them compare the first differing line rather than editing assertions until the program passes. A copy error in JSON, indentation, or punctuation should be corrected from the visible source. After the run, have them open both saved JSON files. The first represents the genuinely read-only lookup task. The second is a write-capable demonstration state whose pending and unknown markers deliberately block resume.

Read the result rows before the detailed traces. All baseline designs succeed in two steps, proving that early termination is real. Empty execution uses five interleaved steps, five fixed workers, and ten reflection steps across exactly two trials. Changed execution fails in every design because no matching OPEN incident is observed. Then inspect the all-empty trace. Interleaving alternates based on evidence and attempt counts. Plan-first execution fills five declared slots without replanning. Reflection completes Trial 1, evaluates, writes one lesson, passes that memory into Trial 2, and stops at the trial limit. There is no invented third trial and no tool action after termination. Close by reading the persistence rows. The read-only task may resume. The pending and unknown write demonstration may not.

Use the changed case as independent practice. In the interleaved runner, confirming the customer makes the incident the only missing requirement, so later actions keep checking the incident within the bound. In the fixed plan, customer slots still run even after the customer is known because Workers do not replan. In bounded reflection, the stored lesson changes the starting tool in Trial 2, but that change does not invent evidence. The incident still fails. This illustrates why reflection is not guaranteed improvement. Then calculate input growth aloud. Add twenty-four synthetic character-units per accumulated step to the fixed twenty. The five interleaved inputs sum to four hundred sixty. Planner, workers, and solver sum to one hundred twenty. Reduce the ratio to twenty-three over six. State clearly that these units are not measured tokens, prices, latency, or paper benchmark results.

Finish the practical unit with adversarial checks. An OPEN record with the wrong identifier is not success. A scalar observation violates the tool contract. A sixth interleaved step, sixth worker, or third reflection trial violates a declared bound. A task-identity mismatch blocks restart even if the rest of the file looks plausible. Pending and unknown effects also block restart. Ask learners to run two mutations and predict the guard before executing. Emphasize that a failing assertion is useful evidence when a learner intentionally violates an invariant. It shows where the system refuses unsafe state. Also repeat that the fictional tools are read-only. The separate write demonstration teaches blocking and reconciliation, not rollback. Editing the local JSON would not reverse an external effect.

Allow six minutes for learners to annotate the empty traces, solve the changed task, inspect persisted state, and run two negative mutations. Circulate and ask them to justify each stop reason from the declared bound.

Begin the knowledge check when learners can distinguish context-only thoughts from tools, explain why fixed planning can fail before observation, separate reflection memory from weights, and state a verifiable restart rule.
